Current ideation present; intent absent; plan absent; access reviewed true. Disposition: Outpatient care with close follow-up. C-SSRS screen: wish to be dead on several days in the past month; no active thoughts of suicide, intent, plan, preparation or past attempt. Risk factors reviewed without detail: a father who died by suicide, other deaths by suicide in his family, heavy drinking, depression, repeated head injuries, chronic pain, and firearms at home. Lethal-means counseling about firearms was done respectfully, as a hunter's safety question rather than a judgment: he chose to have his guns held in the locked storage at his shooting club while his mood and drinking are treated, and to keep no ammunition at home. A written safety plan was made with him, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in his phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit.

text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Alcohol: AUDIT and DSM-5-TR assessment, brief intervention in his own terms, naltrexone 50 mg daily, thiamine, a drinking diary, a goal he chooses and revisits, withdrawal precautions if he stops (no abrupt stop at his intake level without a plan), and mutual-help or counseling options offered
  • Hepatology consultation for raised iron studies and liver tests in a heavy drinker: to confirm the cause, stage the liver, and plan treatment
  • Hemochromatosis: weekly phlebotomy of 500 mL with a hemoglobin check before each, to a ferritin of 50 to 100 ng/mL, then maintenance; MRI with liver iron quantification and elastography instead of biopsy; no iron or vitamin C supplements, no raw shellfish; no alcohol advised while iron is high and the liver is healing; HFE and iron testing offered to first-degree relatives through a letter he may share, with no result recorded here
  • Depression: PHQ-9 at each visit, weekly psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral therapy) with the clinic's behavioral health clinician, sertraline, the Mood Disorder Questionnaire before the antidepressant, a structured safety assessment with a written safety plan, lethal-means counseling about firearms, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit
  • Post-concussion symptoms: symptom-based care (headache plan without daily analgesics, sleep routine, graded activity, writing in shorter sessions), MoCA repeated after three months with less alcohol, no routine brain imaging without warning signs, and neuropsychological testing if thinking does not improve; chronic traumatic encephalopathy not diagnosed
  • Hypertension: home blood pressure monitoring, amlodipine, less alcohol and salt, ECG and urine albumin at diagnosis, echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension, and a target below 130/80 mmHg
  • Prediabetes: HbA1c repeated at six months, less alcohol, activity and diet; iron overload and alcohol both raise the risk of diabetes

resource.title: Ernest Hemingway synthetic care plan
resource.description: Several conditions that make each other worse, met in one man without judgment: a 55-year-old writer with severe alcohol use disorder, a year after a concussion with a skull fracture, whose routine intake tests show iron overload. The episode covers the diagnosis of hereditary hemochromatosis by transferrin saturation, ferritin and HFE genotyping; staging the liver with elastography and MRI instead of biopsy (AASLD 2011, ACG 2019); weekly phlebotomy to a ferritin of 50 to 100 ng/mL; avoiding iron and vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish; why alcohol multiplies the liver risk of iron overload; offering testing to first-degree relatives without attributing results to anyone; the AUDIT, DSM-5-TR criteria, brief intervention and naltrexone, with the patient choosing his own drinking goal (APA 2018); depression treated with psychotherapy and a carefully chosen SSRI (VA/DoD 2022); a structured suicide-risk assessment with respectful lethal-means counseling about firearms and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (VA/DoD 2024); post-concussion symptoms managed by symptom (VA/DoD 2021) with cognitive screening and no diagnosis of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which can be confirmed only after death; hypertension (CMID, ACC/AHA 2017); and diabetes screening.
